Strip away all the mythology surrounding the Norwegian Method, and what remains at its core is precise intensity control over long periods of time-control that permits high training volume at the right, specific load. Not precision in the sense of "correct pace today," but precision in the sense that week after week you hit an internal load the body can tolerate, one that shifts capacity upward without the muscles gradually becoming the limiting factor.
This is also where most mistakes occur when people try to copy the method, especially double threshold training. They copy the structure but not the control system that made the structure possible. You can always push through a hard session. You cannot push through 40 weeks at slightly wrong intensity without paying the price—whether through stagnation, overload, or injury.
With high precision, the method yields high reward at low risk.
With low precision, high risk and low reward.
This chapter addresses how you actually control intensity at a technical level-not merely by finding the threshold, but by understanding curves, slopes, drift, error sources, and deviation patterns. The goal is for you to make decisions in real time during sessions and adjust correctly before you lose the rhythm of the week. This chapter is intentionally technical.
Breakpoint versus Zone
Before going further, a fundamental distinction that shapes everything that follows: the firen, a twen a true breakpoint and a zone.

Lactate is an indirect measure influenced by factors such as heat, glycogen availability, and measurement uncertainty. We cannot really speak of one certain breakpoint, even though the term is widely used and this book repeatedly refers to it as a "threshold." That is a simplification I am fully aware of.
Because intensity in the Golden Zone is set more conservatively than in many other training philosophies, it helps avoid real accumulation of load and fatigue from sitting right above the anaerobic threshold. This is one reason the method transfers so well for people switching from other approaches, even those claiming to be threshold-based.
The risk of setting one fixed intensity—for example, half marathon pace that sits right at the threshold—is that you will likely spend portions of the session above the load you should be at, due to the factors mentioned above.
You walk straight into overload risk, little by little, week after week.
Read the Golden Zone, then, for what it actually is: a zone. Conservative.
Safe. Effective. The safety margin is deliberately chosen, precisely because the inherent error margins demand it, to ensure you do not become too aggressive in your sessions. I mention this at the outset because I am fully aware of the debate around zones versus breakpoints. To put that discussion to rest:
I believe there is a training zone that is far more beneficial than others, both in terms of effect and load. And in my experience, it is both relatively specific and relatively narrow.
The Adaptation Period
Understanding that we are working with a zone rather than a fixed point leads naturally to a practical question: where should you start if you are new to this kind of training?
In earlier articles on my website, I described my experience of setting threshold session intensity below 3.0 mmol/L from the very beginning if you are not already well-versed in threshold training. I call it a normalization period, or adaptation period.
I still stand by this. Suppose your true threshold, measured in a lab, is 4.0 mmol/l, and you have little experience with threshold training. I strongly recommend setting your threshold sessions consistently in the typical Golden Zone of 2.3-3.0 mmol/L for four to six months before retesting.

For most people, this works surprisingly well for adapting the body to this new type of load. I suspect muscular factors play a role. With poor muscle condition-which most people have—and inadequate training load over time, the threshold tests at 4.0 mmol/L.
What I observe, though, is that even when 4.0 mmol/L is correctly measured at that moment, staying there often doesn't work-despite it being the measured value and despite continued threshold training.
In a sense, by continuing to train at that level, you carry with you whatever caused the threshold to sit at 4.0 mmol/L in the first place.
This small detail can actually cause athletes to abandon the model before they have really gotten started. Ir is a purcly practical adjustment, withour being able to fully explain it physiologically, and unsurprisingly, something no scientific studies have addressed.
Basic Session Management
Once you have established your working zone, the next step is learning how
to manage individual sessions within it.
Before a session, you should have a sense of the acceptable training zone once pace has stabilized. I often speak of 2.3-3.0 mmol/Llactate for many well-trained athletes, but this can easily extend to 2.1-3.3 mmol/L, as long as you are well recovered beforehand, and as long as you treat the ceiling and floor as signals to adjust, not targets to push against.

I recommend starting the session with a short warm-up followed by a single threshold effort of five minutes. This effort both warms up the system and provides vital information about how the session will go. Here is what it
typically tells you:
If heart rate rises quickly, pace is high, and lactate is low, that is the most reliable indicator that the body is primed for the session ahead. If heart rate is somewhat lower at the start but rises toward the end of the effort, pace is high or normal, and lactate is normal, this indicates high receptivity but with some muscular fatigue. It is precisely the muscular sluggishness that causes the heart rate response to lag, in my experience. Not a red flag, but worth noting.
In both cases, the session can proceed normally, and you can even add extra volume toward the end if the curve permits it. With the second scenario, you will more often see the curve rising toward the end of the session. If so, consider scheduling an extra easy day the following week, as this type of profile suggests emerging fatigue.
The Lactate Curve: What You Are Actually Reading The warm-up effort gives you a first indication of what to expect, but the real information emerges as the session unfolds. When you profile or measure during a session, you are essentially reading four things.
Baseline and early response
Some athletes get slightly higher early lactate than expected if the warm-up is too short, if they start too aggressively, or if they enter the session already revved up stress, caffeine, poor sleep. The warm-up effort described above addresses this and gives a useful picture of your current state.
I therefore recommend one to two threshold efforts of five minutes before sessions, as both a control mechanism and adaptation before the main work.
There is also a delayed lactate response, given its nature as an indirect measure, and this ensures a gradual buildup.
The curve's breakpoint and slope
A more distinct lactate breakpoint or accumulation signal can be useful, but the slope is more important. When the slope becomes steeper, you are in a range where a small pace increase requires disproportionately greater anaerobic support. This is precisely what makes threshold sessions unpredictable if you set intensity slightly too high—you can feel "okay," but metabolically and muscularly you are accumulating a bill that comes due 24-72 hours later.
There are exceptions. In some sessions, you will see an initially steep curve that quickly normalizes and flattens. Compare this against heart rate to check for deviation or balance. As mentioned earlier, quick heart rate rise, high pace, and low lactate is the ideal.
My experience is that in such sessions, muscle tone and elasticity are almost always close to optimal. The body is then highly receptive to training load. In a buildup period, this means you should clearly add extra running efforts to the session. In a peaking phase, you may choose to maintain the same session volume anyway, simply to bank that surplus.
An obvious risk of adding more training to sessions where the body is highly receptive is that pace, load, and session length naturally become tougher.
At such full green-light sessions, it is therefore important to take the easy day afterward seriously, using every available tool to normalize the muscles. If you come out of that day with extra soreness or elevated tone, do not be afraid to add an extra easy day.
This is something many miss. During peaking phases and highly receptive periods, it is important not to be afraid of extra rest days to consolidate the hard sessions. This can yield enormous performance gains. At signs of overload or peak readiness, pay extra attention to rest days.
Stabilization in the working range
The "good" threshold session is further characterized by finding a plateau after one to two efforts where lactate stabilizes near the desired level, and then maintaining that stability by adjusting pace minimally. This range will often be a zone of perhaps 0.3-0.6 mmol/L lactate, within which you move freely.
Drift through the session
Drift means lactate gradually rises even though pace remains the same. You hold the same tempo, but the curve creeps upward. Drift can be caused by heat, fluid loss, low fuel in the muscles, heavy surface, stiff muscles, or pauses that are too short. We must never forget that lactate is an indirect measure of load--though by a wide margin the best one readily available. Moderate drift can be acceptable. Steep drift at the same pace is a red flag—you are either too high, or the body is not receptive that day.
In sum, you train not just by numbers, but by curve shape.

An Operational Interpretation System:
The Five Session Types
These four elements-baseline, slope, stabilization, and drift-combine to produce recognizable patterns. Over years of profiling, I have come to classity sessions into five distinet types, each with its own implications for how you should respond.
The principle is simple: in practice, we measure lactate in the blood, not inside the working muscle. What we see is the net result of two simultaneous processes: lactate appearance and lactate removal. Lactate is formed primarily in working muscle when glycolytic flux is high and pyruvate is reduced to lactate to sustain energy production, and it is removed through uptake and oxidation in the heart and oxidative muscle (including oxidative fibers within the working muscle), as well as conversion to glucose in the liver.
Lactate is transported out of more glycolytic fibers largely via MCT4 and taken up by oxidative tissues largely via MCTI. These transport pathways are trainable, and well-trained athletes typically have a higher capacity to both export and import lactate than untrained individuals.
The curve therefore tells as much about transport and balance as about how hard the session is. The goal then becomes choosing intensity that delivers a high training effect at the lowest possible biological cost.
For classification to have value, some standardization is needed. You do not need a laboratory, but you need a consistent method. Choose a target range rather than a single value. Use a window you want to stay within during efforts.
Take samples at fixed time points after maintaining a steady pace. You want to see trends, not noise. Look at change over time at the same load.

Decision Rules in Practice
Knowing the five session types is one thing; knowing what to do with them in the moment is another. Here are the decision rules I have found most usefu
over the years:
1. Stabilize before you build volume
On long threshold efforts (for example, 6 × 2000 m) measure at least the fist two to three efforts to ensure you are in the right range. Once the value stabi-lizes, you can either "lock" the session or continue measuring.
Continuing to monitor is best, but if cost is a concern, choose to measure at the very start. Supplement ideally with measurements toward the end. The advantage of continuing to measure throughout the session is all the information it provides about current state, especially regarding session extension.
With repeated "green signals," I recommend adding extra running efforts, for example, one to two intervals at the very end.
2. Adjust pace cautiously
During lactate-guided sessions, it is rarely about dropping ten seconds per kilometer (16 seconds per mile). It is often about two to five seconds per kilometer (3-8 seconds per mile), or small adjustments in rest intervals and rhythm. If you must make large adjustments to hit the right lactate, either your form that day or standardization is off, and then it is often better to modify the session rather than force it into a template.
3. A clearly rising curve at the same pace is a stop signal with exceptions
If lactate rises repetition after repetition at the same pace and same pause, you have in practice already left the threshold range. You can "complete" by pushing, but then you have turned the session into something else, with a different cost.
For a model that must tolerate two threshold days per week and often double threshold, this is a poor trade.
There are, however, some exceptions. If you have completed a slightly too demanding session just before, or a hard race, this can show up in the curve,
precisely because tone is elevated.

In those cases, I have found it useful to continue the session to lower tone further, while still accumulating sufficient volume. I would then recommend lowering lactate from 2.3-3.0 mmol/L down to just above 2.0 mmol/L. This is then concluded with Smart Strides-smooth running efforts of 80-100 meters just above the threshold to break things up. You are then choosing to change intention within the threshold session itself.
I consciously used this principle after races, sometimes doing this directly after races with threshold efforts set somewhat lower, or the day after. You then accumulate threshold load, but with a slightly different intention-to lower muscle tone while still incorporating some elements of threshold training during a period when it must be balanced against more intensive training.
4. Use heart rate as a secondary signal
A high threshold heart rate combined with controlled lactate can indicate that the system is "open" and that the aerobic engine can work hard without tipping over.
For coaches, this means that if you use heart rate naively as a ceiling, you may at times limit athletes who are actually running well. Heart rate must be interpreted together with lactate curve, pace, and muscular response.
An amusing digression here: the renowned physiologist Stephen Seiler is mentioned in the training chapter regarding his contribution on 80/20 training. He lives only 1.7 km (about a mile) from me in the small city of Kristiansand—I can almost see his house. Several years ago, I had a conversation with him about precisely my observations on heart rate and lactate. He confirmed the theoretical basis for this and suspected, as I had observed, that braking mechanisms were likely involved.
We are back to the body's protective system.
Is it safe to open all the gates here?
In principle, though, this requires two things. First, that you do it with muscles that are actually functioning well. Second, with a body that has enough general surplus to allow opening up in that way. The duality is important to understand, and especially important in a peaking phase.
5. Use perception as a tertiary signal
Subjective perception, whether RPE or the extended talk test as described in Chapter 2, should be used actively throughout. This is the simplest signal to add, and it captures imbalances in the system, given that no measurements or models are completely accurate. Additionally, you should keep using the stair test and traffic light model, to provide a complete picture of receptivity.
Variation within the Lactate Range
The decision rules above assume you are aiming for a stable target, but there is also room for deliberate variation within the Golden Zone itself.
In the first article I wrote in 2021 about the Norwegian Method, I described parts of an intense experimentation phase within the Golden Zone:
*   Progressive sessions where lactate progressively increases from around 2.0 to 3.0 mmol/L over the course of the session, interval by interval.
*   Sessions where I would hold just below and up to 3.0 mmol/L and push this level as long and hard as possible.
*   "Floating" sessions where I would sit 0.4-0.8 mmol/L below the threshold.

Adjusting Long Intervals
Even with careful planning, sessions sometimes go off track. If during long intervals you get several efforts with lactate that is too high, you realistically have three choices: end the session, markedly reduce the load and restart the curve, or switch to shorter intervals.
All alternatives are possible, but often the most beneficial is to either end the session or switch to shorter intervals. The choice depends on two things.
First, what did your traffic light model show before the session? Check resting heart rate, HRV, warm-up heart rate, and ideally the stair test. If you were borderline and start missing on the curve, I recommend ending the session.
Alternatively, you can run some 30/30 intervals (30 seconds on, 30 seconds off) to break things up muscularly before trying again.
Second, if the parameters looked fine, it depends on where you are in the season. If you are approaching a tougher training period or the competition season, I recommend switching to shorter intervals. This can correct muscular imbalances that are beginning to build up, while maintaining some aerobic volume. If you are in the middle of winter in a buildup phase, the alternative may instead be to restart the curve with a lower starting pace.
If you choose this, I recommend accepting a flat curve for the rest of the session, at a slightly lower lactate level, to avoid risking another untavorable Lactate Measurement into Competition Season Everything discussed so far applies primarily to base and buildup phases. As you move toward competition, the picture becomes more complex.
Earlier in the chapter on the ambitious athlete, I mentioned the importance of also being able to interpret lactate values during the summer season and competition season. The curve reveals a great deal about how early the body turns to anaerobic pathways, in my experience. Therefore, curve interpretation of longer intervals above the threshold during the transition and competition
season itself is extremely important.

Additionally, as you approach peak form, it is useful to monitor heart rate alongside lactate. You want heart rate during threshold sessions to gradually increase, with pace rising correspondingly, just before peak form arrives. You have then hit the balance between surplus and performance.

He warns that some athletes testing lower lactate levels could not always be a good thing because it may be coming at a greater cost to the opposing system. Do you have any thoughts on that or advice on how to tell with individual athletes?"
And then a follow-up question: "Did you ever experiment with fluctuations of pace to manipulate the threshold? For example, either fartlek, or 200 meter on/off for longer threshold reps if you could achieve correct lactate values? Canova seems obsessed with the on/off pace change for everything, but I wonder if there is something to slightly spiking the lactate and then lowering it while still moving slightly slower."
These are very interesting questions for anyone training athletes at a high level. I appreciate both of these thought processes, and as mentioned earlier, an ideal system for elite athletes should probably contain elements of both aspects noted above. The challenge is, again, implementation in a safe manner and weighed against the core principles of the model.
I advocate simplification almost down to a primitive focus on what probably yields the greatest gains, before moving outward from there into experimental phases.
Choice of experimental elements should be athlete-specific and intention-spe-cific. We can, however, use lactate actively to accomplish this as safely as possi-ble. If an on/off model is used, lactate should be measured during the session.
This is challenging and must be done with assistance, and always at the same point in the active pauses.
The opposing systems question ties directly to the thinking about the two horses from Chapter 6 and drip load from the same chapter. This is also partly sport-specific. Running demands extreme muscular caution, and it is the only form of movement we carry from early childhood, with the impact loading that implies. We have narrower margins to work with here compared to many other sports.
As a Norwegian, I am very familiar with the training of cross-country skiers and the necessity of more dynamic work within sessions, because the terrain demands variation, especially in hills. One element is that the upper body is also used, but at the same time, if we applied the same intensity variation to a pure running session, the recovery time would be far longer.
We must always keep in mind the specific demands that running presents.
The Long-Term Thinking on More Intensive Training
These advanced considerations lead naturally to the question of how intensive training fits into the broader picture.
At the foundation lies a threshold-based focus. On top of this, there will always be a fixed element of more intensive training, but the frequency can vary. For some recreational runners, this can actually be done with weeks between sessions, with only focus on easy running and threshold training; for well-trained athletes, once a week as a template of sorts.
The fixed intensive element is thus fully open to individual planning.
Beyond this, elements like speed training and strength training, as well as potentially more than one intensive session per week (such as two sessions over a ten-day period), will be individually determined and phase-dependent. More explosive athletes will often tolerate this better; likewise, gradual adaptation over time builds tolerance far better than abrupt integration.
The reason I outlined such a simple transition from base training to competition season in earlier chapters, with short intervals that gradually become Longer at a lactate of 7-10 mmol/L, is because it provides a safe model that works for most people. Most people will make mistakes in this transition phase, and that is why I am conservative in my advice. That is also why this may appear
"too simple" compared to more complex models like those described above.
But if you constantly weigh training against your threshold value, factor in your muscular state, and understand how high your threshold pace must be for necessary performance, you can and should systematically think through the composition of more intensive sessions. For some, this will entail far greater amounts of intensive work in a session. For others, somewhat increased fre-quency. For others still, increased complexity.

Changing these variables requires monitoring the following closely:
*   The lactate curve within the intensive session—which systems does it trigger?
*   Adaptation to the given session —how the body responds when you repeat it over weeks, and how it affects threshold sessions in the same period.
If you run on/off training and see dramatically better lactate values within the session at a given pace week after week, while the curve is flat (meaning the aerobic pathway) and the threshold value remains stable in sessions before and after these more intensive sessions, this type of session gives you adaptations that are beneficial, underdeveloped, and may be worth focusing on further.
Again, you always stand at the fixed center and move outward with curiosity, but always with load, control, evaluation, and adjustment as guiding princi-ples. Experimentation with the model should be timed and phase-dependent.
I personally chose to use the fall each year for three to four months of extreme experimentation, before gradually returning to known elements.
Lactate Values during Experimentation
When experimenting with more intensive work, you also need guidelines for acceptable lactate ranges. Given a threshold value of around 3.0 mmol/L, my experience is that you should experiment in the 5-7 (8) mmol/L zone first.
There is enough stimulus here for real effect, while it is far safer than higher zones. As always, risk is weighed against reward
Practical Sample Collection
All of this depends, of course, on getting reliable lactate measurements in the first place. Lactate measurement in the field is simple in theory but full of potential errors in practice. The greatest cause of measurement errors is not the meter but user error in sample collection. Here is what you need to know to get reliable values.
Where should you prick?
You have two choices: fingertip or earlobe. Both work, but they do not give identical values. Blood samples from the fingertip show consistently higher lactate values than samples taken from the earlobe at the same time. The difference can be significant, with an average deviation in some studies of 0.66

mmol/L, and up to 0.86 mmol/L in the 4-8 mmol/L range. But even in the threshold range, the difference is substantial.
For running and cycling, research recommends the earlobe. During training on an ergometer or treadmill, there were no significant differences between venous samples and capillary samples from the ear, while fingertip values were higher. The earlobe may be preferred because it is less affected by lactate release from the arms and easier to sample.
The problem with the earlobe is that it requires a helper. If you are testing yourself, you must use the finger. The important thing is that you choose one site and stick to it. Do not compare values from the finger one day with the ear the next. Personally, I ran with the lactate meter in my pocket during sessions and pricked my own finger carlobe samples were impossible to manage alone.
Contamination is often the main problem
Sweat has much higher lactate concentration than blood and can significantly alter the reading. A single drop of sweat that mixes into the blood sample can give a completely wrong value. Contamination appears to be the single largest cause of measurement error. The smaller the blood sample the meter requires, the more likely contamination from sweat or oil on the skin becomes.
The protocol that works
Dry the area thoroughly with a towel or paper towel first. Remove all visible sweat from finger or ear, and preferably from hand and arm as well, since sweat can run down. Then clean with an alcohol swab and let the area dry completely before pricking. Alcohol residue can also contaminate the sample. After prick-ing, wipe away the first drop of blood to avoid contamination. Wipe away the first drop with a clean swab and test on the second.
Cold fingers give poor samples
In cold conditions, peripheral blood flow to the fingers drops, which can make sampling slow and readings less reliable. Some runners also have chronically poor finger perfusion. If your ngers are cold even at room remperature, use the earlobe.
Correct drop size
The blood drop should be round and stand up from the skin, not flat and runny.
If the sample is thin and watery, do not use it. A watery drop may mean contamination with sweat, or that the athlete is overhydrated. The drop should be 2-3 mm in diameter. If you do not get enough blood after ten seconds, prick again next to the original site instead of squeezing hard. Squeezing presses out tissue fluid that dilutes the sample.
Summary in Practice
What does all of this add up to in daily training? You establish a working range for threshold training, not a single threshold pace. You establish a connection between pace, heart rate, and lactate on a standardized day. You use profiling regularly to detect shifts. The curve moves to the right, or becomes steeper at the same pace. What you want is a robust way to set threshold sessions that deliver high aerobic load but low risk of the session escalating. You want a system that tells you when to push and when to hold back, before the body forces you to.
But the tool is only as good as its use. A lactate meter in the hands of someone who does not understand curve shape, drift, and error sources can do as much harm as good. The number alone says little. It is the change over time, the relationship with heart rate and pace, and the pattern through the session that give you the information you need.
It takes time to become good at this. You will miss things. You will misin-terpret. You will have sessions where you see in hindsight that you should have adjusted earlier. Over time, you build experience-how your body responds under different conditions, which patterns warn of problems, and which signal that you can push more. When it clicks, you can train more without the same cost. That is the entire point.
And once you can control intensity this precisely, the next step is obvious:
two quality sessions in one day, both kept inside the Golden Zone.
That is double threshold.

*   ZONE, NOT BREAKPOINT. The Golden Zone is deliberately conservative-typi-cally 2.3-3.0 mmol/L for well-trained athletes. In Chapter 7, I introduced double threshold for runners training four to six hours per week. In the chapters for the ambitious runner, I laid out concrete weekly structures with specific sessions. This chapter goes deeper, not into how you do it, but into why it works.
If you had to choose one thing that separates this approach from traditional training, it would be double threshold: two threshold sessions on the same day, repeated weekly, with strict intensity control. Getting there took years.
I experimented, failed, adjusted, measured, and adjusted again.
What I ended up with was not theory first and practice afterwards. I found something that worked, and the understanding came later. Two sessions done correctly function as a single block-the total physiological cost less than the sum of its parts.
The mechanism is not one single thing. Double threshold exploits the timing of the body's stress response, the behavior of muscle tone across hours, and the specificity of threshold-pace running to deliver more total stimulus at lower total cost. Each of those elements matters on its own. Together, they explain why this structure can be sustained week after week when other high-volume approaches cannot.
Most runners who try double threshold and fail do so for the same reason: they get the format right but the control wrong. They run too hard in the morning session, arrive depleted for the evening, and accumulate a stress load that looks like two separate hard days compressed into one. That is the opposite of what the model intends.

Done correctly, the two sessions function as a single block where the total physiological cost is less than the sum of its parts.
Understanding why requires looking at three things: the limitations in training load, the limitations in performance, and the principles of adaptation and specificity.
Parts of this chapter draw on my article "Double Threshold in Depth," which covers the three pillars, the NTNU study, and the Radcliffe data in fuller detail and will be expanded. This chapter assumes that foundation but goes further in two directions: the load equation, which reframes how the body actually accounts for training stress, and the connection between double threshold and muscle tone, which I could not adequately address without the preceding chapters of this book.
If you already use double threshold and want to understand the underlying mechanisms, this chapter is for you. If you are still finding your way into the method, the earlier chapters are enough. You can always come back.

Limitations in Training Load
The ceiling for training load in running comes down to two things: the general stress response (cardiovascular, hormonal, nervous system) and the muscular stress response. Double threshold addresses both, but I have come to believe the muscular component is the decisive factor.
The General Stress Response
You can overtrain by doing too much of everything. With enough overall load, regardless of stimulus, the body will say stop. But in the Norwegian Method, you are protected by the threshold intensity itself. In the Golden Zone between 2.3 and 3.0 mmol/L lactate, stress hormone activation is far lower than with harder sessions. You do not drive the body into full stress mode. You extract enough stimulus to signal adaptation while remaining in full control. You push metabolic and hormonal systems hard enough to trigger change, but not so hard that the signal becomes damage.
Because the general stress response is kept well within manageable limits, you can increase training frequency within the weekly framework. And as I describe below, parts of the stress response are delayed, so double threshold also protects against overtraining at loads that would otherwise carry risk. This gives you an ideal starting point for what really matters.
The Muscular Stress Response
Here is something I have thought about for years: why can cross-country skiers and cyclists maintain high-intensity load over far longer durations than runners? The central physiological systems are taxed equally across these sports.
The primary difference is muscular impact.
This distinction does not get enough attention. Too much focus goes to
"general load" rather than identifying what actually differs between activities, and between running intensity zones in particular. Within the muscular system, you face two challenges that are crucial for understanding the double threshold model. First, muscle damage and soreness—the general wear and tear, typically experienced as delayed soreness. Second, muscle tone and clasticity-the subtle but critical changes in tension and responsiveness that accumulate across training days.
Double threshold provides a system where you accumulate significant stimulus while managing both factors effectively. By keeping intensity at the threshold rather than pushing harder, you minimize how much you train while carrying muscle soreness. By placing two sessions within a single day, you work with natural recovery rhythms rather than against them. Muscle tone after the first session actually prepares the system for the second.
Why the Stress Response Comes Late
A central reason that blocking works is the timing. The soreness and structural stress response runners experience are delayed. Delayed onset muscle soreness typically peaks around 24-72 hours and subsides over 5-7 days. Biomarkers tell the same story: creatine kinase and myoglobin peak within 24-48 hours, sometimes remaining clevated 48-72 hours after the effort. The immune response is also time-shifted, with leukocyte infiltration and inflammatory signaling unfolding over hours to days.

What double threshold actually does is exploit a receptive training window, before these responses kick into full gear. In my experience, the body treats the two sessions as one long stress load rather than two separate ones. The full inflammatory response only hits the day after, and that day is kept very easy.
I tried countless variants with threshold work every day, mainly sub-threshold.
The cumulative stress effect was the same. Overtraining came quickly.
But since double threshold is so controlled, and the following day is exclusively easy, the body enters a cycle of controlled stress followed by specific adaptation, followed by enough rest for the system to calm down. In my experience, this type of double work does not add much extra recovery time.
You get far more training without a corresponding increase in recovery needs.
This means two things. During the double threshold day, your tone will be fine for the second session—the morning session acts as a primer rather than adding load. And the time to return to lower tone on the easy day afterward is shorter than expected.

The Load Equation
The NTNU study 1 cited earlier offers more than a comparison of two training structures. It reveals something about how the body accounts for load.
As mentioned, in 2024, Kjøsen Talsnes and colleagues at NTNU conducted the first systematic comparison of one long threshold session versus two shorter ones the same day. Let us look a bit closer at it. The study, published in Frontiers in Physiology, included 14 well-trained endurance athletes with an average vO,max of 69.2 ml/kg/min. Each athlete completed both protocols: a single session of 6x10-minute intervals, and two separate sessions of 3x10-minute intervals with 6.5 hours of rest between them. Intensity was set at 90 percent of the speed at 4 mmol/L. Total workload was identical.
The lactate response was the most striking finding. In the single long session, blood lactate rose progressively from around 2.60 mmol/L in the first half to 3.01 mmol/L in the second half. This gradual accumulation is what researchers call lactate drift, indicating increasing metabolic stress as the session con-tinues. With the double protocol, something remarkable occurred: lactate actually decreased from the first session to the second. The morning session produced values around 2.72 mmol/L, while the evening session dropped to 2.14 mmol/L-despite this being the second threshold effort of the same day.
Heart rate followed the same pattern. In the long session, heart rate climbed by approximately 5 beats per minute from first to second half— classic cardiac drift caused by reduced stroke volume, rising core temperature, and progressive recruitment of Type Il muscle fibers. With double threshold, the response reversed: heart rate fell from the first to the second session. When comparing the final 30 minutes of the single session to the corresponding second session in the double protocol, the difference reached 6-8 beats per minute lower with the split approach.
Perceived exertion diverged as well. On the Borg scale, athletes in the single session reported progressive increase from 13.4 to 14.8 through the workout. In the double protocol, perceived exertion stayed relatively stable around 13-14 in both sessions. The final 30 minutes of the long session felt significantly harder than the corresponding minutes in the evening double session. This difference in perceived load carries direct implications for how frequently such sessions can be absorbed.
Recovery markers completed the picture. During the 60-minute post-session window, supine heart rate was higher after the single session-about 65 bpm compared with 61 bpm after the split protocol. The following morning, athletes rated fatigue higher after the split day: 8 versus 7 on the study's I-to-10 scale, where higher means better recovered. Muscle soreness followed the same pattern, 7 versus 6, again favoring the split approach.
Same volume. Less cost.
My own experience with evening lactate values was identical. Typically you arrive at the second session with a body that is remarkably receptive-lactate running lower in the evening despite the morning's work still in your legs. It comes down to muscle tone and delayed stress response not having fully set in yet. In a sense, you get the full benefit of the morning session without paying for it in the evening.
The practical implication is straightforward. If you can achieve the same or greater training effect at lower physiological cost, you can do more of it, not in any single session, but across the week and across the months. This is the load equation that makes double threshold viable.
The researchers framed it carefully: lower strain per session "could allow more accumulated time at this intensity." They stopped short of claiming superior adaptation, since the study measured acute responses rather than longitudinal outcomes. But the implication aligns with what I have observed across years of testing. Runners who structure threshold work as concentrated blocks with genuine recovery between them tolerate more total volume than those who spread the same work across isolated sessions with incomplete recovery in between.
There is a second implication buried in the data. The reduced lactate in the second session of the double protocol may reflect partial glycogen depletion from the morning work. I return to this below.

While VO_max tends to plateau with sufficient training over time, the anaerobic threshold continues to improve with the right stimulus. This is where double threshold excels.

The Research Perspective
In the review article "Does Lactate-Guided Threshold Interval Training within a High-Volume Low-Intensity Approach Represent the 'Next Step' in the Evolution of Distance Running Training? which I co-authored with physiologist Carl Foster and former European 1500-meter champion Arturo Casado, we addressed precisely this question.
The hypothesis is that training near vLT2 improves muscle-specific adap-tations, including lactate clearance as opposed to reduced lactate production.
Since only recruited motor units experience increases in mitochondrial number and capillary density, training near vLT2 may optimize the number of motor units recruited without the consequences of elevated catecholamines likely experienced with z4 training.
The Radcliffe Case
This point is well illustrated by data on Paula Radcliffe, documented in Andrew Jones's 2006 study "The Physiology of the World Record Holder for the Women's Marathon." The study traces her training and test results over a 12-year period toward one of the greatest performances in endurance sports history: her 2:15 marathon.
The data reveal something important. The largest performance improvements do not necessarily come from a higher ceiling, but from speed at high aerobic intensities moving upward while running economy improves. Rad-cliffe's VO,max ranged from around 65 to 80ml/kg/min across years, but when multiple tests within the same year are viewed together, it appears relatively stable at approximately 70 ml/kg/min from 1992 to 2003. The capacity at the top was extremely high, but it did not become dramatically higher throughout her development.
What clearly shifted was running economy. The oxygen cost at 16 km/h fell from approximately 205 ml/kg/km in 1992 to approximately 175 ml/kg/ km in 2003, an improvement of around 15 percent. In later measurements it was reported even lower, around 165ml/kg/km. When running economy improves without VO,max rising correspondingly, the same physiological load converts to higher speed.
The same pattern appears in the lactate profile, where the curve shifts to the right over the years. Speed at 3 mmol/L went from 16 km/h in 1992 to 21 km/h in 2003, while her threshold speed rose from 16 km/h to 20 km/h.

Jones notes that a cornerstone of Radcliffe's training philosophy was that she never compromised quality for quantity. Easy runs were done at 5:15-5:45 per mile, controlled and steady. Tempo runs near the threshold for 20-40 minutes were a fixed part of the program.

The Performance Rationale
For well-trained runners, this provides a clear rationale. VO,max may be relatively stable for long periods. When it is, further performance gains come through better running economy and higher threshold speed-higher speed at a high percentage of VO, max. Training must therefore not just raise the ceiling, but move race pace upward at a load that can be repeated often enough to drive real change.
This is where double threshold becomes logical. The method accumulates significant time near the threshold, but at a controlled internal load that allows quality to be repeated week after week. If you can execute multiple threshold stimuli per week without the total load tipping over, you create the conditions for threshold speed and economy to move gradually upward. These are precisely the parameters that separate performance when VO,max is already high.

The Principles of Adaptation and Specificity
As described earlier in the book, you want to stimulate a sufficient number of relevant motor units aerobically to improve pertormance. This is central to everything. The specificity of the method lies in achieving this in the gentlest way possible, through volume.
The volume provides two advantages:
First, the recruitment pattern at the threshold captures a broad spectrum of fibers needed for racing, because the speed is close enough to race pace to be relevant. You train these motor units thoroughly, not in passing.
Second, you accumulate far more time at controlled speeds resembling race-pace movement than most other models allow. That accumulated time builds efficiency that transfers directly to competition. The result is a rare combination: high adaptation and high specificity, at a cost the body can absorb week after week.
The Pace Spread Advantage
To optimize this further, adjustments can be made within the framework.
An often-overlooked advantage of the morning/evening structure is the pace spread. Morning sessions at the threshold are typically 1-2 percent slower than evening sessions. Add the difference between longer intervals in the morning and shorter ones in the evening, and the range can reach 15-20 seconds per kilometer (24-32 seconds per mile), all within the threshold zone on a given day.
This is why I recommend longer intervals in the morning and shorter in the evening. The spread gives the body a broader adaptive range: you build the ability to hold steady pace over longer periods and responsiveness at higher speeds. Both are directly relevant for racing.
Additional Adaptive Benefits
There is also a possibility that this type of training concentration produces additional adaptive effects. Part of the reason for lower lactate in the second threshold session of the day may be a slight depletion of glycogen from the morning session. Running in that state in the evening can trigger adaptive changes and introduce a specific element of metabolic stress that proves beneficial —without adding any further mechanical load to the muscles.
This presents an opportunity to vary your approach through the year. In winter, running the evening session in a state of slight depletion can amplify the adaptive response. The body learns to perform when fuel stores are partially drawn down-a useful adaptation for endurance, and one that comes at no
additional mechanical cost.
In summer, I would aim for the opposite. Be as fully fueled as possible before the second session, since the goal shifts from building to sustaining.
Build as little as needed, not as much as you can. Keep the muscular system tuned for racing while balancing against more intensive and riskier sessions.
Reload glycogen aggressively after the morning threshold work.
One practical option is to fuel during the final interval in particular and continue through the cool-down. The glycogen loading potential during activity exceeds that at rest, since active muscles absorb fuel more readily.
The window is open. Use it.
Additional Specific Variations
As mentioned in Chapter 6, several variants exist for those who want to stretch double threshold training further. These mostly involve manipulating rest periods and interval length across a much wider range than most runners are accustomed to.
But you can also use the priming effect of the morning session before a more intense evening session. This works particularly well when the evening session targets a lactate range of 5-8 mmol/L in the weeks before the racing season. A morning threshold session at the very lower end of the zone—say 1.7-2.5 mmol/L-provides both threshold stimulus and a preparatory effect that enhances the quality of what follows. The body arrives at the harder session already activated, already warm in a metabolic sense. The evening work lands differently than it would on fresh legs.
The point in all of this is simple: as long as you stand at the center and look outward, understanding the goals, benefits, and limitations, be creative. This applies to double variants as much as anything else in the model.

Elements of Increased Complexity
Beyond the classic twice-weekly double threshold structure, three aspects deserve particular attention.
Maximum Build versus Minimum Sustain
During winter training and the buildup phase, you use double threshold to extract maximum load from your training pushing limits with the best possible control, as described above.
But if you have experience with double threshold and understand the
NTNU findings, you will recognize that the approach can also serve as a minimum-load strategy. The structure of the NTNU study essentially splits threshold work into two sessions, resulting in less total stress per session. This means you can add more to both sessions if building, but it also means you can get the work you need at lower cost if sustaining.
This aspect is often overlooked. Andreas Almgren has understood it. He uses double threshold in summer as well, but with shorter sessions and lower intensity —and an even greater range between morning and evening efforts. Instead of a single 6-7x6-minute threshold session to sustain fitness during competition season, he runs perhaps 4-5x6 minutes in the morning and 15-20x1 minute in the evening. Same or greater volume, substantially less stress. The structure also permits more recovery time between hard days, providing the energy reserves needed during peaking. He uses double threshold to sustain and sharpen simultaneously.
Splitting Weekly Intensive Load
This applies particularly to recreational runners, though I have observed it in elite athletes as well. If your work involves extended static postures during the day, placing double threshold on weekends— then using easy running to lower tone from accumulated workplace stress during the week-often works better than spreading quality sessions across weekdays when you arrive already fatigued.
I have seen this pattern repeatedly. You must respect overall muscular load, and that includes demands outside of running. Double threshold placed on days when vou are rested and ready works far better than threshold work on davs when vou are worn down. Do not underestimate the priming effect a well-executed morning session creates for the evening run.

I have also observed runners structure their weeks as: double threshold Tuesday, easy Wednesday, rest Thursday, easy Friday, then double threshold or threshold morning plus X-session evening on Saturday, followed by longer easy runs Sunday and easy Monday. This distributes the hard training days with more spacing between them. You still complete four quality sessions weekly, but with additional recovery days.
For certain individuals, this structure provides precisely the extra rest the
weekly cycle demands.
Dynamic In-Season Adjustment
The competition season requires its own calibration-maintaining the threshold foundation while adding race-specific sharpening without tipping into overload. The governing principle remains constant: the phase adapts to the framework, not the other way around.
In practice, this means that as the X-session becomes more intensive and race-specific through spring and summer, the double threshold days should become lighter, not abandoned, but recalibrated to serve a sustaining rather than building function.
You also want to be much more dynamic. Use double threshold sessions on and off, depending on your needs. If you notice a drop in aerobic capacity that does not correct itself after backing off training for a few days to a week, you may need to trigger the aerobic system again. In that case, re-introduce double threshold if you have dropped it.
You may even run double threshold twice a week for 1-2 weeks in-season, just to trigger the system while giving more recovery between the days, entirely dropping the more intense work. In that case, slightly longer easy runs can also help—again to normalize muscle tone. By doing this you get three things at once: more aerobic load, less anaerobic triggering, and longer runs to normalize tone in the absence of anaerobic work. You also reduce general stress by spacing the hard training days further apart. The sum of this can save the racing-season.
The point is: in season, use double threshold actively and deliberately.

Practical Implications for the Advanced Runner
If you already have experience with double threshold and want to optimize further, here are the most important points:
*   Prioritize the character of the morning session. The morning session sets the tone for the entire day. Longer intervals (6-10 minutes) keep muscle tone down and prepare the system for the evening's higher-fre-quency work. Go too hard or too short in the morning, and you destroy the conditions for what follows.
*   Structure the week around muscle tone variation. Think not just about load in hours and kilometers, but about how muscle tone varies through the week. The easy days are as much about lowering tone as about cardiovascular recovery.
*   Use the pace spread deliberately. Do not see the difference between morning and evening pace as a problem. See it as a training advantage. You build a broader adaptation foundation.
*   Keep the evening session disciplined. Even if you feel better in the evening (as many do), that is not a signal to push harder. Lower lactate at the same subjective effort means the system is receptive, not that you should increase the load.
*   Respect the timing. Six to eight hours between sessions is my preferred window. Shorter can work, but you lose some of the benefits of muscle adaptation. Longer than ten to twelve hours, and you begin approaching two separate sessions rather than one block.
The Big Picture
The power of double threshold training lies in how load, limitation, and structure work together. You accumulate substantial training volume at a pace close enough to race pace to drive specific adaptations, while keeping the load controlled enough to avoid the accumulated stress response that leads to overtraining.
You work within the body's natural recovery rhythms, using muscle tone dynamics to your advantage rather than fighting against them. And you systematically push the threshold, the real performance limiter for most long-distance runners, higher and higher, week after week, with a body that remains ready.

This is why the model works, not because of one simple mechanism, but because it addresses multiple limiting factors simultaneously and creates a training system that is both highly effective and remarkably sustainable. At least, that is what decades of testing and observation have taught me. And it is impossible to fully understand without considering muscle tone, which is the subject of the next chapter.

Most training books stop at load and intensity. This chapter goes further, into territory that is harder to write about but no less important. It is technical, and difficult to explain without precision. But I know many readers are curious, and I believe it deserves its own chapter in this in-depth part of the book.
In Chapter 4, I explained why the muscular system is often the true bottleneck in running. Here we go deeper: what muscle tone, elasticity, and stiffness actually are, why they change, and how you can influence them.
I noticed the muscular system's role early, but it was physiotherapist Johnny
Høgseth who opened the door to something more precise.
When I was competing, I was notorious for my obsession with brief massage sessions. During the final two years of my career, studying medicine while competing at the Olympics, European Championships, and World Championships from 2004 to 2006, I often sat between lectures with my hands wrapped around my thigh, working the muscles while my classmates laughed. I wanted to understand what I was feeling, not just practically, but theoretically.
Professor Per Brodal was a leading figure in Norwegian neurology and a former dean at the Faculty of Medicine. His landmark textbook, The Central Nervous System (1990), contained a brief passage noting that muscle tone is influenced by both afferent and efferent activity, but that much remains unclear.
Afferent nerves carry sensory information into the brain and spinal cord. Efferent nerves carry signals out to muscles and other organs.
Together with a fellow medical student, I showed up at his office. We asked if he would supervise our master's thesis: a pilot study measuring muscle tone objectively with a myotonometer after massage, combined with a literature review.

Brodal's response: "I notice with age that fewer and fewer topics truly interest me. But this is interesting."
That thesis became the academic foundation for how I understand muscle tone today. It connected with years of practical experience I had already accu-mulated. Toward the end of my career, my focus shifted increasingly toward optimal muscular condition, alongside an increasing volume of double threshold training. That shift in attention never left me.
Three Core Concepts
Before we continue, three concepts need to be defined. They are fundamental to understanding how muscles respond to training and load.
Muscle tone is baseline tension-how tense the muscle is. It is influenced by nervous system regulation and the mechanical properties of muscle and connective tissue. Resting muscle tone is the baseline tension when the muscle is not voluntarily activated. You can feel it as resistance to passive movement. It is determined by the interplay between low-grade neural activity, the muscle's viscoelastic properties, and structural components of the tissue. When we speak of increased muscle tone after hard training, we mean the muscle is holding higher baseline tension than normal.
Muscle elasticity is the tissue's ability to return to its original length after being stretched. In running, this manifests as a spring effect in the muscle-tendon unit: elastic energy is stored on landing and released in the push-off. The muscle fibers primarily produce force and regulate tension and timing. Elasticity comes especially from titin in the muscle fibers and collagen-rich connective tissue surrounding them. The cross-bridges between actin and myosin create force and increase active stiffness when the muscle engages. When this works optimally, energy is stored and released in a stretch-shortening cycle, and running becomes more efficient.
Muscle stiffness is the resistance the tissue offers against applied force-how much the muscle resists being stretched, compressed, or deformed.

Higher stiffness benefits rapid stretch-shortening cycles and high-velocity movements because it makes force transfer more efficient, but stiffness is also a risk factor for injury, especially when it climbs too high over time without
adequate recovery.
How They Relate
Tone, elasticity, and stiffness are closely connected but measure different things.
Tone tells you how tense the muscle is. Elasticity tells you how well it returns to normal length after load. Stiffness tells you how much it resists being stretched or compressed during movement.
When training is optimal, tone is moderate, elasticity is high, and stiffness is balanced. When you slide into overtraining, tone climbs, elasticity drops, and stiffness either spikes or paradoxically collapses. Add any adhesions between muscle bellies, and the interplay degrades further. The result of optimizing this is enormous.
I still have periods when I use old knowledge to adjust muscle tone and elasticity, structuring training better, managing intensity, combining it with massage and heat. During these periods, I work the muscles toward the reference point I know so well. The result? I can run 20-30 seconds faster per kilometer (32-48 seconds per mile) at the same effort. That kind of improvement would take years to achieve through fitness alone.
Everything in this book-the training structure with easy runs, double threshold, massage, hot baths, avoiding static load— has one goal: to keep you as close to this muscular reference point as possible.

The Muscular Reference Point
My interest in muscle tone has bordered on obsession. The combination of an elite running background and work as a physician means I've palpated thousands of running legs. I can be reserved in many areas. When it comes to muscle tone, I've been relentless, driven by the need to understand something so central to performance yet so rarely described anywhere.
I've felt the muscles of 100-meter sprinters who have broken 10.00. Karsten Warholm's thighs. Henry Ronos, when he attempted a comeback as a masters runner. Craig Mottram, my competitor who finished third at the World Championships in 2005 as the only non-African besides me. And countless East African runners at the very top of the world.
During medical school, I worked at a physical therapy clinic specializing in overtraining, doing cross-friction massage and assessing athletes in every phase of performance. I was broke after years of lactate measurements, altitude equipment, and extended stays in Kenya. The clinic work kept me afloat.
Then came general practice, where health conversations sometimes turn to performance. Around 5,000 consultations a year, 65,000 over thirteen years.
Maybe one in five involves a muscular problem where palpation is essential: to diagnose, understand, and treat. You develop a feel for tissue.
It is the same with children who arrive with sports injuries, and with hunting dogs. That last one may require explanation. Or perhaps not, because here is the point:
Children, hunting dogs, and the world's best runners share the same muscular reference point. Almost no one else comes even remotely close.
It sounds comical, but the pattern is unmistakable. The fantastic elastic fullness in the muscles, the renewability, perfect stiffness and optimized yet dynamic tone, varying somewhat by phase and exercise type.
This quality is extraordinarily rare in regular runners, and I believe it shouldn't be.
As elite athletes approach peak form, their muscles become increasingly homogeneous. At maximum performance, given normal training over time, it's almost always optimal muscular condition that emerges as the deciding factor.

Practical Optimization
Practical muscular optimization divides into two categories: active influence and passive influence.
Active Influence: Training Structure
Active influence is the training itself. Generally, higher speed, higher intensity, and more static load will increase muscle tone. A tough hill session with high intensity, somewhat more static load, and relatively high speed will therefore be far more demanding than many other session types.
But as mentioned, there's something else many runners don't realize: higher intensity doesn't just raise muscle tone more—it also extends the time required for tone to return to normal. And the pattern is often unpredictable. You lose control of the recovery window. Sometimes an easy day before the next hard session works fine, while other times it doesn't.
This unpredictability is one of the hidden costs of intensive training. With a threshold-based model, you keep this under far greater control.
The Structure of the Norwegian Method
The weekly structure I developed leverages muscle tone systematically during the base training period.
THE ORIGINAL SETUP:
One reason for this structure. Tuesday with 6 × 2000 m in the morning and 25 x 400 m in the evening, is that the morning session with longer repetitions doesn't raise muscle tone nearly as much as the evening sesston. The interval length makes the difference.
The double threshold sessions place longer intervals in the morning delib-erately, to avoid pushing tone too high throughout the day. At the same time, those morning intervals act as a primer; the muscles become more ready for the evening session, not less. The shorter evening intervals allow variation in pace while remaining under full control.
Week after week, one easy day between double threshold sessions is suffi-cient, given appropriate load and sufficient buildup over time. Predictability in weekly structure means fewer transitions, which means predictability in muscle tone.
The longest threshold intervals of the week are placed on Thursday, precisely so that tone is not already elevated going into the weekend. Then comes the tougher session, the X-session, often hill work.
The day after the X-session brings an easy but somewhat longer run. Easy intensity combined with slightly more distance is perfect for lowering tone as much as possible after hard hill work. Monday adds another easy day, meaning total muscular recovery time is two days, not one.
